title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Colorado confirms foreign actors changed settings, silenced alarms and altered pumping at two small water systems
items.content_text: Colorado’s Governor’s office said on 18 September that foreign actors breached two small, privately owned drinking-water providers in late August, changing equipment settings, disabling alarms and remote access, and altering pumping cycles. The state says the disruptions were brief, the providers corrected them and alerted the state, and there was no known effect on treatment, water quality or public safety. The office cannot confirm which actors were involved, though it points to a known Iranian-backed campaign against water and wastewater systems; The FBI declined to comment, and Denver Water says its own systems were evaluated and are unaffected. Why this matters: the national campaign against internet-exposed water controllers now has hands-on process tampering confirmed by a state government rather than inferred. Each utility serves fewer than 200 people — and at that size, the alarm the intruders switched off is often the only operator on shift.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Colorado Governor’s office statement, reported by Reuters, AP, Axios Denver, the Denver Post and KRDO; context from CISA, FBI, EPA and NSA advisory AA26-097A
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Intrusions late Aug 2026; disclosed 18 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

items.title: The Coast Guard and FBI boarded two tankers over suspected cyberattacks — part of 40 to 50 cyber missions in a year
items.content_text: US Coast Guard and FBI personnel boarded two Texas-bound oil tankers in late August after indications that the vessels’ networks had been breached during the voyage. Rear Adm. Amy Grable, who commands Coast Guard Cyber Command, told CBS News that reviewing the IT and other onboard systems of the Liberian-flagged crude carrier VL Prosperity did turn up evidence of a malicious cyber actor, but that nothing found suggested the ship was unsafe to operate. Iranian state media claims the intrusion reached the engine room — slowing coolant flow, raising engine speed, interfering with fuel delivery and cutting communications for about 30 hours — and those claims remain unverified; the Coast Guard has not attributed the incident to Iran. The detail worth sitting with is Grable’s: this was one of an estimated 40–50 cyber missions the Coast Guard’s Cyber Protection Team carried out in the past year.
tags: Incident — confirmed malicious cyber activity aboard two US-bound tankers; no confirmed operational disruption; attribution unresolved

items.title: A US-loaded LNG carrier turned away from its discharge port after losing control systems — and the crew say the valves were being driven from somewhere else
items.content_text: The Liberia-flagged LNG carrier Vivit Africa, loaded at Cameron LNG in Louisiana and bound for Rovigo, Italy, lost access to some internal control systems as it approached the Adriatic in early September. The Italian Coast Guard confirmed it assisted the vessel after the master reported a malfunction affecting cargo-parameter monitoring; the ship never discharged and instead sailed for Algeciras, Spain. Crew members separately told the trade press that attackers took temporary control of steam pressure and safety valve systems near Gibraltar and later of tank pressure controls and relief valves in the Adriatic. Officials have not established a cause and no attribution has been offered. For OT defenders the value here is the shape of the claim, not its verdict: the systems described are the ones that keep a cargo inside its safe envelope, and they are reachable from the same integrated automation network as the monitoring that failed.
tags: Incident — confirmed control-system malfunction aboard an LNG carrier; crew claim cyber manipulation of pressure and relief valves, cause not established

items.title: A cyberattack stopped container handling at Tanjung Pelepas — and the restart ran on paper and manual gate-ins
items.content_text: The Port of Tanjung Pelepas in Malaysia detected a cyber incident affecting its terminal operating systems late on 9 September and suspended container-handling operations as a precaution. A phased restart began the following day, with some export gate-ins processed manually while systems were recovered; the operator says container operations have since resumed. PTP is an MMC Group and APM Terminals joint venture that moved 14.03 million TEU in 2025, which puts it among the largest transhipment hubs anywhere. For OT defenders this is the cleanest recent example of the pattern that actually causes industrial downtime: the attack did not need to reach a crane PLC or a straddle carrier to stop the boxes moving — taking out the system that decides where every container goes was sufficient.
tags: Incident — confirmed cyberattack on terminal operating systems; container handling suspended at one of the world’s largest transhipment hubs

items.title: Settra hit a manufacturer, cleared the logs and disabled recovery — and the responders could not establish how it got in
items.content_text: Huntress detailed a September intrusion at a manufacturing company by the newly identified Settra ransomware variant, alongside a July case at a retail and consumer-services firm. In the manufacturing case the responders observed a vulnerable signed driver used to disable security controls, encryption, clearing of Windows event logs and disabling of recovery options — and were not able to establish the method of initial access. In the July case at the other firm they found the MeshAgent remote monitoring tool used for persistence. No OT impact was reported, and that is precisely the point worth making to a plant manager: the chain contains no industrial protocol, no controller exploit and no ICS knowledge, yet it lands on the systems production depends on.

items.title: CenterPoint Energy confirms a breach through an external-facing system — service unaffected, but the utility found out from a leak post
items.content_text: CenterPoint Energy, the Houston-based electric and gas utility, filed an 8-K on 14 September confirming it became aware of a third-party post claiming to hold CenterPoint customer data, and that an unauthorised party did obtain personal information through one of its external-facing systems. The company states that delivery of electric and gas service was not impacted. The poster claims roughly 7.5 million records including names, account and billing data, driver’s licence numbers and partial Social Security numbers; CenterPoint has not confirmed that figure or the authenticity of the dataset. From an OT standpoint this is an IT-side breach with no operational consequence — but the sequence is the part worth noting internally: the utility learned of it from a leak post rather than from its own detection.
tags: Incident — utility breach confirmed via SEC 8-K; customer data taken through an external-facing system; electric and gas delivery not impacted

items.title: Porting a PLC exploit to a different model took an AI agent eight hours and about $536 — and it bricked the second PLC
items.content_text: Forescout researchers used an AI coding agent, with heavy human steering, to port a working pre-authentication remote code execution exploit for a Nucleus FTP stack overflow from a WAGO 750-852 PLC to a WAGO 750-831, with no source code and no debugger, and executed attacker-supplied ARM shellcode on live hardware. The final stage alone took eight hours and thirty-two minutes and roughly $536 in model spend, and a follow-up attempt to build a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the test PLC. The researchers’ conclusion is deliberately unglamorous: PLC exploitation has not become easy. What has changed is the marginal cost of moving an exploit across related devices — which erodes the very common decision to deprioritise an OT bug on the grounds that weaponising it would be too much trouble.
tags: Research — Forescout Vedere Labs ported a working PLC exploit between WAGO models using an AI agent; 8h32m and roughly $536

items.title: Twelve flaws in a Siemens edge processing box chain to root — the device that sits between your PROFINET segment and everything else
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its research on the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 Local Processing Engine, identifying twelve vulnerabilities in firmware below V4.0 HF0, with three more affecting other configurations including the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client. The reported issue classes cover privilege escalation, path traversal, authentication bypass, command injection and buffer overflows, several of which chain to root-level control — which on this class of device means telemetry manipulation, alarm suppression and a foothold for attacks against the OT network behind it. Siemens has no fix for some of the findings; the published workarounds are restricting access and disabling the PROFINET DCP service. One presentational note: the identifiers attached to this research are 2025-series CVEs appearing in a September 2026 write-up, which is legitimate — Siemens and CISA advisory activity for this device dates back to 2025 — but it means part of this is a fuller public account of older findings rather than wholly new disclosure. Check the identifiers against Siemens ProductCERT before raising a change record.
tags: Research — Nozomi Networks Labs: 12 vulnerabilities in the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 local processing engine; chainable to root

items.title: A 720-page incident-response framework just went free — and one of its chapters is about control systems
items.content_text: SANS published Dynamic Incident Response: A Framework for Security Teams by SANS Fellow Joshua Wright on 15 September, the first substantial rebuild of the SANS incident-response framework in roughly twenty years. It is 720 pages across twenty chapters, free in every digital format under a Creative Commons licence, and the model it introduces — DAIR, a Dynamic Approach to Incident Response — aligns to NIST guidance and the Cybersecurity Framework while abandoning the assumption that response proceeds through neat sequential phases. Three chapters are contributed: Dean Parsons on operational technology and control systems, Megan Roddie-Fonseca on cloud, Ryan Chapman on ransomware and extortion. For OT teams the value is less the model than the availability: there is now a current, citable, no-cost reference with a control-systems chapter that you can put in front of a plant manager, an engineering lead or a procurement reviewer without a licence conversation.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: SANS Institute announcement; book available free at dynamicincidentresponse.com
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 15 Sep 2026 — verified 21 Sep 2026

items.title: Manufacturing ransomware is up 40% and the victim has moved to mid-market Europe — which changes who your supplier risk is
items.content_text: Black Kite counted 1,183 new manufacturing ransomware victims between January and July 2026, a rise of roughly 40% on the same period in 2025, and 5,237 disclosed victims since January 2023. Half of this year’s attacks came from groups that did not exist two years ago; one new crew alone accounted for 12% of them. The geography moved sharply: European victims rose 85% — Germany 77, Italy 57, the UK 43, France 40 — while US volume was flat, dropping the US share from 52% to 35%. For anyone running a supply-chain risk programme, the practical consequence is that your exposure has shifted toward mid-market European suppliers who are less likely to have an OT security programme, a tested recovery plan, or the ability to tell you quickly that they are down.
tags: Report — Black Kite: 1,183 manufacturing ransomware victims through July 2026, up ~40%; European victims up 85%; half from crews under two years old

items.title: The box that decides which VLAN a device lands in can be taken by an unauthenticated request — and it is being taken
items.content_text: Cisco disclosed a maximum-severity authentication bypass in Identity Services Engine and the ISE Passive Identity Connector, tracked as CVE-2026-76460 at CVSS 10.0, caused by insufficient authentication control on an API endpoint. An unauthenticated remote attacker can bypass the web management interface and gain unauthorised access to the device. Cisco says it was exploited as a zero-day; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 16 September with a federal remediation deadline of 19 September, now passed. There is no workaround — upgrading is the only remediation, with fixes in ISE 3.5 P4, 3.4 P7, 3.3 P12, 3.2 P11 and 3.1 P12. For industrial sites, ISE is frequently the thing enforcing which devices land on which VLAN, including the boundary between enterprise and plant. Whoever holds ISE can rewrite that boundary without touching a switch, a firewall or a controller.

items.title: Two SonicWall SMA1000 flaws chain to unauthenticated code execution — and where compromise is suspected the advice is to reimage and rotate
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed two flaws in SMA1000 secure remote-access appliances on 1 September: a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Work Place interface at CVSS 10.0, and a post-authentication OS command injection in the Appliance Management Console at CVSS 7.8. Rapid7 reports the pair chain to unauthenticated remote code execution on an appliance that is normally internet-facing by design. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2 September. SonicWall published no indicators of compromise and told customers to contact support to review appliances for signs of intrusion and, where compromise is suspected, to re-image or redeploy, rotate all credentials and reset TOTP tokens — which tells you what the vendor thinks the realistic post-exploitation state is. This is the fifth KEV-listed SMA1000 defect since December 2025, and ransomware crews including INC and Akira have repeatedly used SonicWall gear as an entry point into environments that include plant networks.
tags: Advisory — CVE-2026-83548 (CVSS 10.0 pre-auth SSRF) and CVE-2026-83549 (CVSS 7.8 post-auth OS command injection), SonicWall SMA1000; chained and exploited in the wild, both in KEV

items.title: Siemens protection relays leak enough to calculate a valid session ID — authentication bypassed on substation feeder protection
items.content_text: Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 covers nine newly assigned 2026 vulnerabilities in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays running firmware below V2.70, alongside several older third-party identifiers carried in the same advisory. The most serious, CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4.0 9.3, exposes enough information through the device web interface for an unauthenticated network attacker to calculate current and past session identifiers and bypass authentication entirely. The set also includes a low-entropy session token, an HTTP resource-exhaustion denial of service that reboots the device, and a memory-corruption issue in firmware-update mode. CISA republished it as ICSA-26-258-05 on 15 September and its own SSVC scoring marks the flaw automatable. No exploitation has been reported. This is the most sector-specific item on the page for electric utilities: these are feeder protection relays, and a relay that can be reconfigured or rebooted is a protection-system problem, not an IT one.

items.title: An authentication-algorithm flaw in Modicon M580 — including the Safety variant — when the project runs at a lower application level
items.content_text: Schneider Electric’s 8 September advisory SEVD-2026-251-04 discloses CVE-2026-3869, an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm (CWE-303) in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, carrying CVSS v4.0 9.2. The condition applies when a project with a lower application level is running: all M580 below application level 4.00 and all M580 Safety below 4.20 are affected, with potential loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability of the controller. No CVSS v3.1 score has been published. CISA’s enrichment records exploitation as none and automatable as no, and the EPSS score is very low. The detail that matters operationally is the application-level condition: many sites are running older project files on newer firmware without realising that the authentication behaviour follows the project, not the controller.

items.title: The OEM maintenance tunnel runs commands as root, survives reboots, and keeps working normally while it does
items.content_text: CISA republished IXON’s advisory as ICSA-26-246-02. The IXON VPN Client’s local configuration interface accepts changes without authenticating the requester, and values written to a configuration file consumed by a privileged subprocess are not neutralised for line endings. Chained, an attacker can inject additional directives and execute commands as root on Linux or SYSTEM on Windows, tracked as CVE-2026-75925 at CVSS v3.1 9.6. The two details that make this an OT problem rather than an endpoint problem: the injected configuration persists across reboots, and the VPN carries on working normally afterwards, so there is no user-visible sign. CISA lists the affected sectors as commercial facilities, critical manufacturing, energy, information technology, and water and wastewater — which is a fair description of everywhere an OEM installs a remote-maintenance tunnel.

items.title: One crafted CIP message crashes RSLinx Classic — and on Logix controllers it forces a fault that needs a power cycle
items.content_text: CISA published a run of Rockwell Automation advisories on 1 September. ICSA-26-244-01 covers four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic up to and including 4.50 — CVE-2026-9621 and CVE-2026-9622 at CVSS v3.1 8.6 / v4.0 9.2, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 at 7.5 / 8.7 — all reachable across the network by an unauthenticated attacker, all triggered by a single crafted CIP message, all crashing the RSLinx Classic service. In practice that is loss of view for every HMI and historian client using that comms server. ICSA-26-244-03 covers CVE-2026-9637 at CVSS v3.1 7.5 / v4.0 8.7: improper CIP length validation can drive a Logix controller into a Major Non-Recoverable Fault requiring a physical power cycle, with the companion ICSA-26-244-05 covering ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix. The safety controllers are in scope, and an MNRF on a GuardLogix is a production stop.
tags: Advisory — CISA ICSA-26-244-01 / -03 / -05; Rockwell RSLinx Classic and the Logix platform; unauthenticated CIP denial of service, one packet, no known exploitation

_otthreatfeed.category: Advisory — CISA ICSA-26-244-01 / -03 / -05; Rockwell RSLinx Classic and the Logix platform; unauthenticated CIP denial of service, one packet, no known exploitation

items.title: A kernel bug in the box that aggregates your plant data — any workload already on the node can become root
items.content_text: ABB Ability Edgenius ships a Linux kernel carrying CVE-2026-31431, an incorrect in-place operation in the kernel’s algif_aead cryptographic interface where source and destination mappings differ. A locally authenticated user — or a container workload already running on the node — can invoke that interface, trigger the faulty memory handling and escalate to root, which means arbitrary code execution, full control of the node, or making it unavailable. CVSS v3.1 7.8, CVSS v4.0 7.3. ABB fixed it in Edgenius 3.2.4.1 and CISA republished the advisory on 17 September. It is not remotely exploitable on its own, and that is exactly how it should be read rather than filed: Edgenius is a containerised edge platform that aggregates process data and carries it northbound, so it habitually sits with one interface on the plant network and one facing the enterprise or cloud. This flaw converts “an app on the edge box misbehaved” into “the edge box belongs to someone else.”
tags: Advisory — CISA ICSA-26-260-06 / ABB: Linux kernel flaw in Ability Edgenius lets a local account or container workload reach root on the edge node

items.title: A hard-coded key protects AVEVA pipeline project files, and app passwords are hashed with MD5 — read access is enough
items.content_text: AVEVA’s September advisory, republished by CISA as ICSA-26-253-01, covers four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor. A hard-coded cryptographic key (CWE-321) protects PIMBoards project files, so anyone with read access to those files can decrypt their contents; CVE-2026-81821 carries CVSS v4.0 8.3 (v3.1 8.4). Separately, application-native user passwords are hashed with MD5 (CWE-327, tracked as CVE-2026-81822), so the same read access allows offline brute-force recovery and escalation to PIMBoards administrator. Two further identifiers, CVE-2026-81823 and CVE-2026-81824, are referenced in the same advisory. All versions prior to 2025 SP1 P2 are affected. No exploitation has been reported. The practical exposure here is a file-share permission problem as much as a software one — pipeline integrity project files are routinely stored where engineering and contractors can read them.

items.title: The grid supply-chain order names RTUs, PLCs and safety systems — and lets DOE make you isolate or replace gear already installed
items.content_text: Executive Order 14420, signed 26 August, declares a national emergency over foreign-produced bulk-power system equipment and prohibits acquiring, importing, transferring or installing such equipment tied to designated entities where the transaction was initiated after that date. Scope is transmission at 69 kV and above — local distribution is explicitly excluded — and covers transformers, inverters, generators and battery storage and industrial control systems: remote terminal units, programmable logic controllers and safety systems, together with associated firmware, software and remote-access capability. For equipment already installed, DOE can require operators to identify, isolate, monitor, secure, disconnect or replace components, and may publish a pre-qualified vendor list and negotiate mitigation agreements. No country is named in the order. The order gives DOE 120 days to publish implementing regulations, and until those rules land no individual transaction is formally prohibited — so the scope being written this autumn decides how expensive the fleet-level question becomes.
tags: Policy — Executive Order 14420: national emergency on foreign-produced bulk-power system equipment; ICS explicitly in scope; DOE implementing regulations due within 120 days

items.title: The Coast Guard now has one office that owns maritime cyber policy — and it is enforcing while the boardings continue
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard has stood up a dedicated Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy as the single central authority for cyber policy across the Marine Transportation System — ports, vessels and MTSA-regulated facilities. Created under the Director of Inspections and Compliance, the office will write domestic policy, feed international standards work, direct a unified compliance and enforcement strategy, and act as primary liaison to industry, other agencies, academia and the national laboratories. It arrives roughly eighteen months after a February 2025 GAO report criticised the Coast Guard on incident-data accuracy, access to cyber deficiency findings, strategy alignment and MTS cyber competency requirements; the Coast Guard has not linked the two. Read alongside the tanker boardings on this page, the direction is unmistakable: maritime cyber has moved from guidance to inspection and enforcement, with one office now owning both.
tags: Policy — US Coast Guard establishes the Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy as central authority for ports, vessels and MTSA-regulated facilities

items.title: CISA’s answer to living-off-the-land: put things on the network that nobody has any legitimate reason to touch
items.content_text: CISA published guidance on 16 September on deploying cyber decoys — tripwires, breadcrumbs and honeytokens — inside internal networks and systems, explicitly framed around adversaries who use stolen valid accounts, built-in administrative utilities and other living-off-the-land techniques that produce no malware to detect. The logic is simple and unusually well suited to OT: a decoy credential, API key, document, database record or cloud token has no role in normal operations, so any interaction with one is a high-fidelity alert rather than another entry in a queue. The guide maps decoy placement to MITRE Engage and ATT&CK and walks through planning, implementation and refinement at low complexity. The part worth flagging to budget-constrained plants: CISA tells organisations to repurpose EDR, identity and data-loss-prevention tooling they already own to deploy and monitor decoys, not to buy a deception platform.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA guidance, corroborated by CyberScoop and Industrial Cyber reporting

items.title: EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting is live — 24 hours to tell ENISA about an actively exploited flaw, including in products already sold
items.content_text: From 11 September, the Cyber Resilience Act’s Article 14 reporting obligations are mandatory. Manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents to ENISA and the relevant national CSIRT on a staged clock: early warning within 24 hours, technical notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days for an exploited vulnerability or one month for a severe incident. ENISA’s CRA Single Reporting Platform went live the same day. The detail that matters for OT is that this bites on products already on the market, not only new ones, and reaches OT vendors, embedded and IoT makers, networking suppliers and system integrators who substantially modify products. Full manufacturer conformity obligations follow in December 2027.
